questions.question: Which interval condition appears in the Heine–Cantor theorem?
options: $(a,b)$ is a bounded open interval with $a \lt b$.
$[a,b]$ is a closed interval with $a \lt b$.
$[a,\infty)$ is a ray.
$\mathbb{R}$ is the only possible domain.

questions.question: Why does $g(x) = x$ on $(0,1)$ not contradict the Heine–Cantor theorem even though it is uniformly continuous?
options: Because $(0,1)$ is bounded, and boundedness is all the theorem uses.
Because the theorem also covers open intervals, so it predicts this.
Because continuity on a bounded interval always gives uniform continuity.
Because the theorem gives a sufficient condition, not a necessary one.

questions.question: What conclusion does Heine-Cantor draw from continuity on $[a,b]$?
options: The function is discontinuous at both of the endpoints.
The function is constant on $[a,b]$.
The function is uniformly continuous on $[a,b]$.
The function is differentiable on $[a,b]$.

questions.question: What does uniform continuity add beyond ordinary continuity?
options: The function must stay bounded on the whole domain, even near the ends.
The function must be differentiable with a bounded derivative.
A single $\varepsilon$ is fixed for the whole domain instead of each point.
A single scale of input control works across the whole domain.

questions.question: To which of the following does the Heine-Cantor theorem apply directly?
options: $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,\infty)$
$f(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor$ on $[0,2]$

questions.question: Which example shows that in the Heine-Cantor theorem the closed interval $[a,b]$ cannot be replaced by an arbitrary bounded interval?
options: $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,\infty)$

questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,3]$, which is uniformly continuous by the Heine-Cantor theorem. Which rule for $\delta$ guarantees, for every $\varepsilon>0$, that $|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$ for all $x,y\in[0,3]$ with $|x-y|<\delta$?
options: $\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{3}$
$\delta=\sqrt{\varepsilon}$
$\delta=\frac{1}{6}$ for every $\varepsilon$
$\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{6}$

questions.question: To show that a continuous function $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ is Riemann integrable, one shows that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a partition of $[a,b]$ such that on each of its subintervals the values of $f$ differ by less than $\varepsilon$. Which step of this argument needs the Heine-Cantor theorem rather than continuity at each point alone?
options: Finding, for each point $x\in[a,b]$, an interval around $x$ on which the values of $f$ differ by less than $\varepsilon$.
Finding one $\delta>0$ such that on every subinterval shorter than $\delta$ the values of $f$ differ by less than $\varepsilon$.
Showing that for every partition of $[a,b]$ the upper sum of $f$ is at least as large as the lower sum of $f$.
Finding an antiderivative $F$ of $f$ on $[a,b]$, so that the integral equals $F(b)-F(a)$.

questions.question: A student tries to prove that every continuous function $f$ on an interval $I$ is uniformly continuous: fix $\varepsilon>0$; for each $x\in I$ continuity gives some $\delta_x>0$ with $|f(y)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $y\in I$ and $|y-x|<\delta_x$; put $\delta=\inf_{x\in I}\delta_x$; then $|x-y|<\delta$ gives $|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$. Which statement about this argument is correct?
options: The argument is correct: on a closed bounded interval it is the proof of the Heine-Cantor theorem, and other intervals work the same way.
The flaw is that each $\delta_x$ depends on $\varepsilon$, whereas uniform continuity needs a $\delta$ that does not depend on $\varepsilon$.
The flaw is that the infimum need not exist, because the set $\{\delta_x\colon x\in I\}$ may have no lower bound.
The infimum of infinitely many positive $\delta_x$ can be $0$; for $1/x$ on $(0,1)$ the admissible $\delta_x$ shrink to $0$ as $x\to0$.
